_comment: Narration for the three architecture diagrams on site/architecture.html. Every claim here is read off the diagram it accompanies or the source that generated it — no numbers invented for effect, because the audience is a customer who may go read the code. Each cue lights diagram cells by their drawio data-cell-id: "cells" are the boxes being talked about, "links" the connectors between them — split because a connector can be long enough to cross a narrow viewport on its own, and only the boxes should decide where the canvas scrolls. Cues are anchored to a sentence index rather than a timestamp: the player divides each track's measured duration between its sentences the way scripts/demo/make_captions.py times captions, so re-recording the audio re-times the highlights with it. Regenerate the audio with scripts/build_narration_audio.sh after editing.

tracks.text: This is how AxonLLM deploys onto AWS. Traffic from your applications arrives over the OpenAI-compatible API, and identity comes in separately from your own provider over OIDC, SAML, or SCIM — so AxonLLM never becomes another user directory you have to keep in sync. CloudFront fronts the deployment, and an Application Load Balancer terminates TLS and forwards to the gateway. The gateway itself runs as an ECS Fargate service: two tasks to begin with, each 1024 CPU units and 2 gigabytes of memory, scaling out to ten on CPU and request-count targets. There is no server to patch. State lives in a single DynamoDB table, on demand, holding usage records, projects, API keys, the audit chain, policies, and provisioned users. One table, not eight, so a restore is one restore. Provider API keys stay in Secrets Manager and are read at startup — they are never baked into the image and never appear in an environment variable you could accidentally log. Logs go to CloudWatch with thirty-day retention, and the container image is built and versioned in ECR. Everything you see here is defined in one CDK stack, so this diagram is not an aspiration — it is what deploys.

tracks.label: Request Pipeline
tracks.ssml: <speak>This is what happens to a single request. <break time="500ms"/>Every call to the chat completions endpoint runs this same ordered pipeline, and the step numbers on the diagram are the step numbers in the source — including the fractional ones, which are the checks added after the original sixteen and deliberately never renumbered. <break time="600ms"/>The request is parsed and its project and user resolved. Quotas are enforced and max tokens capped, using a policy hierarchy that resolves from organization, to business unit, to project, to environment — so a limit set once at the top applies everywhere below it. <break time="600ms"/>Then the security checks. Prompt injection detection runs on normalized text, so homoglyph and Unicode tricks do not slip past. Personally identifiable information is replaced with tokens before the prompt ever leaves your account, and the mapping is held in memory to be restored on the way back. <break time="600ms"/>Next the limits: rate limiting on a sliding window, model access checked against both the project and the user allow-lists, and budgets checked for each — where the tightest limit wins. <break time="600ms"/>Then the cache. A hit returns right here and never reaches a provider, so a repeated question costs nothing. <break time="500ms"/>Routing has three paths. Direct sends to a named model with a fallback chain. Smart routing classifies the intent, consults a leaderboard, and picks on cost and quality. Ensemble asks a panel of models, takes a quorum, and synthesizes an answer — with the budget pre-checked against the full panel cost, before spending it. <break time="600ms"/>On the way out: response guardrails, the redacted values restored — per chunk, even when streaming — and an entry appended to a SHA-256 hash-chained audit trail. <break time="500ms"/>Finally cost is priced from the table and charged to the project and the user. <break time="400ms"/>The point of this diagram is the count of exits: every one of those steps is a place you can say no before the money is spent.</speak>
tracks.text: This is what happens to a single request. Every call to the chat completions endpoint runs this same ordered pipeline, and the step numbers on the diagram are the step numbers in the source — including the fractional ones, which are the checks added after the original sixteen and deliberately never renumbered. The request is parsed and its project and user resolved. Quotas are enforced and max tokens capped, using a policy hierarchy that resolves from organization, to business unit, to project, to environment — so a limit set once at the top applies everywhere below it. Then the security checks. Prompt injection detection runs on normalized text, so homoglyph and Unicode tricks do not slip past. Personally identifiable information is replaced with tokens before the prompt ever leaves your account, and the mapping is held in memory to be restored on the way back. Next the limits: rate limiting on a sliding window, model access checked against both the project and the user allow-lists, and budgets checked for each — where the tightest limit wins. Then the cache. A hit returns right here and never reaches a provider, so a repeated question costs nothing. Routing has three paths. Direct sends to a named model with a fallback chain. Smart routing classifies the intent, consults a leaderboard, and picks on cost and quality. Ensemble asks a panel of models, takes a quorum, and synthesizes an answer — with the budget pre-checked against the full panel cost, before spending it. On the way out: response guardrails, the redacted values restored — per chunk, even when streaming — and an entry appended to a SHA-256 hash-chained audit trail. Finally cost is priced from the table and charged to the project and the user. The point of this diagram is the count of exits: every one of those steps is a place you can say no before the money is spent.

tracks.label: Components
tracks.ssml: <speak>This is what is inside the gateway. <break time="500ms"/>There are three ways in, and they share one core. The dashboard server runs it as a web service. An AgentCore entry point runs the same gateway as a Bedrock agent. And a command-line interface covers local development and operations. <break time="600ms"/>Behaviour is configuration, not code. The model registry, provider credentials, the pricing table, benchmark leaderboards, ensemble presets, and the hub-and-spoke topology are each a YAML file — so adding a model or repricing a provider is an edit and a reload, not a release. <break time="600ms"/>Three layers of middleware wrap every request, outermost first: authentication, then role and scope checks on the admin surface, then request security. <break time="500ms"/>Identity and access is deliberately made of small pieces: hashed API keys with rotation, JWT and load-balancer token validation, SAML service-provider metadata, SCIM provisioning, and Cedar policies for authorization. <break time="600ms"/>At the centre, the gateway orchestrator holds the pipeline you just saw, including true streaming — the response is streamed straight from the provider rather than buffered and replayed, so first-token latency is the provider's, not ours. <break time="600ms"/>Around it sit the router and its strategies, the provider factory that adapts thirteen providers to one wire format, the quota enforcer and cost tracker, the redactor and injection detector, the audit trail, the webhook dispatcher, and a single persistence layer. <break time="600ms"/>What matters commercially is the shape: each of those is one replaceable component behind an interface. <break time="300ms"/>You are not buying a monolith you have to accept whole — you are buying a set of parts you can audit one at a time.</speak>
tracks.text: This is what is inside the gateway. There are three ways in, and they share one core. The dashboard server runs it as a web service. An AgentCore entry point runs the same gateway as a Bedrock agent. And a command-line interface covers local development and operations. Behaviour is configuration, not code. The model registry, provider credentials, the pricing table, benchmark leaderboards, ensemble presets, and the hub-and-spoke topology are each a YAML file — so adding a model or repricing a provider is an edit and a reload, not a release. Three layers of middleware wrap every request, outermost first: authentication, then role and scope checks on the admin surface, then request security. Identity and access is deliberately made of small pieces: hashed API keys with rotation, JWT and load-balancer token validation, SAML service-provider metadata, SCIM provisioning, and Cedar policies for authorization. At the centre, the gateway orchestrator holds the pipeline you just saw, including true streaming — the response is streamed straight from the provider rather than buffered and replayed, so first-token latency is the provider's, not ours. Around it sit the router and its strategies, the provider factory that adapts thirteen providers to one wire format, the quota enforcer and cost tracker, the redactor and injection detector, the audit trail, the webhook dispatcher, and a single persistence layer. What matters commercially is the shape: each of those is one replaceable component behind an interface. You are not buying a monolith you have to accept whole — you are buying a set of parts you can audit one at a time.
